title: Body parts: what each part of your body helps you do

summary.text: Tape your thumb down, and a grain of rice becomes very hard to pick up. Your fingers are all still there, but they need the thumb to press against. Every part of your body helps you do something: eyes see, legs walk, and joints like the elbow and knee let you bend. Many jobs need two or more parts working together. All people have the same kinds of parts, but each body is a little different. In this unit you name your body parts, tape your thumb and try everyday jobs, and find out what your elbow does.
summary.art: A child's hand with the thumb taped flat to the side, trying to pick up one grain of rice from a steel plate, while the other hand, thumb free, pinches a grain easily.

intro.hook: Touch your nose. Now try to touch your right elbow with your right hand. Can you?
intro.text: Almost nobody can touch their elbow with the hand on the same arm. The elbow bends only one way, so the hand cannot get round to it. Every part of your body helps you do some things. In this unit you name your body parts, find what each one does, and tape your thumb down to see which jobs get hard.
intro.art: A girl twisting and laughing as she tries to touch her right elbow with her right hand, while her grandmother watches.

outcomes: By the end I can name the main parts of my body, from head to toes, and point to them.
By the end I can say one job that each part helps me do, like eyes help me see and legs help me walk.
By the end I can say why my thumb matters, using what I found when my thumb was taped down.
By the end I can say what a joint is, and show where my body bends.
By the end I can say how bodies are alike and how they are different, in people and in other animals.

terms.meaning: A body part is one piece of your body, like your head, an arm, a hand or a foot. Each body part helps you do some jobs.
terms.example: Your eyes are body parts. They help you see.
terms.art: A child standing with arms out, with small arrows pointing to the head, an arm, a hand, a leg and a foot.

terms.meaning: Your thumb is the short, thick finger on the side of your hand. It can bend across your hand and touch the tip of every other finger.
terms.example: When you pick up a grain of rice, your thumb presses against your first finger.
terms.art: A hand with the thumb tip touching the tip of the first finger, in a pinch.

terms.meaning: A joint is a place where two bones meet. Your body bends at its joints.
terms.example: Your elbow, knee, wrist, ankle and knuckles are joints.
terms.art: An arm bending at the elbow, with a small circle drawn round the elbow.

terms.meaning: Bones are the hard parts inside your body. They hold you up and give your body its shape.
terms.example: Press your shin, the front of your leg below the knee. The hard part you feel is a bone.
terms.art: A child's hand pressing the front of the lower leg, with a faint drawing of the long bone inside.

terms.meaning: Muscles are the soft, strong parts under your skin that move your bones. A muscle gets shorter and pulls on a bone.
terms.example: Bend your arm and feel the top of it. That muscle goes hard as it pulls your arm up.
terms.art: A child bending one arm and feeling the top of the arm with the other hand.

explanations.concept: Every part of your body helps you do something
explanations.definition: Each body part helps you do some jobs. Many jobs need more than one part.
explanations.description: Eyes see and ears hear. Your nose smells and helps you breathe. Your mouth eats, talks and sings. Hands hold, legs walk, and skin feels every touch. Most jobs need many parts. To catch a ball, your eyes watch, your arms reach and your hands close.
examples: To eat idli, your eyes find the idli, your fingers break a piece, your arm lifts it and your mouth chews.
To kick a ball, one leg swings while the other leg holds you up.
To sing a song, you use your mouth, your tongue, your throat and your breath.
explanations.context: This card is about the jobs our body parts help us do.
explanations.art: A child catching a ball, with small labels on the eyes (watch), the arms (reach) and the hands (close).

explanations.definition: Your thumb can bend across your hand and press against each finger. Together, the thumb and a finger can pinch and grip.
explanations.description: Your thumb sits on the side of your hand and swings across to meet each fingertip. To pick up a grain of rice, the thumb presses from one side and a finger from the other. With your thumb taped, your fingers could only press on each other. That is why small things and buttons were so hard.
examples: Doing up a button needs a pinch on each side of the button.
Holding a crayon needs your thumb on one side and two fingers on the other.
Apes and many monkeys have thumbs that press against their fingers too. Ours is longer, so it reaches every fingertip more easily.
explanations.context: This card is about the thumb test, where you taped your thumb down and tried everyday jobs.
explanations.art: Two hands side by side: one pinching a grain of rice between thumb and first finger, one with the thumb taped down, the grain slipping between two fingers.

explanations.concept: Joints are where your body bends
explanations.definition: A joint is a place where two bones meet. Bones do not bend, so your body bends at its joints. Muscles pull on the bones to move them.
explanations.description: Bones are hard and stay straight, like a pencil. Where two bones meet, there is a joint, and the joint can move. Muscles pull on the bones, and the bones swing at the joint. With the newspaper tube on your elbow, your arm could not bend, and your hand could not reach your mouth.
examples: Your elbow and knee bend one way only, like a door on its hinges.
Your shoulder can swing your arm round in a big circle.
Each finger bends at three joints, and your thumb bends at two.
explanations.context: This card is about joints, and the straight-arm test, where a newspaper tube stopped the elbow bending.
explanations.art: An arm drawn with the bones showing faintly inside, bending at the elbow, with a muscle on top drawn shorter and fatter.

explanations.concept: Bodies are alike, and each body is different
explanations.definition: Almost all people have the same kinds of body parts. But each person's body is a different size, shape and colour, and works in their own way.
explanations.description: You and your grandmother both have two eyes, a nose and two hands. But her hands may be bigger and more wrinkled than yours. Skin, hair and eyes come in many colours. About one person in ten is left-handed. Some people are born with a different body, or lose a part, and find another way to do the job. Many deaf people talk with their hands, in sign language.
examples: The dancer Sudha Chandran lost her right leg after a road accident in the early 1980s. With an artificial leg called a Jaipur Foot, she danced Bharatanatyam on stage again.
Draw round everyone's hand at home. Every hand has a thumb and four fingers, but no two hands are the same size.
A baby has about 300 bones. Many of them grow together, so a grown-up has 206.
explanations.context: This card is about how people's bodies are the same and how they are different.
explanations.art: Five hand outlines on one big paper, from a small child's hand to a big grandmother's hand, all with five fingers.

explanations.concept: Humans and other animals have many of the same parts
explanations.definition: Humans are animals, and many other animals have body parts like ours. Some animals have parts we do not have.
explanations.description: A crow has two eyes, a beak, two legs and two wings. Inside a crow's wing are bones like the bones in your arm. A cat has elbows and knees, like you. An elephant's trunk is a long nose and upper lip joined together, and the tip of the trunk can pick up a single peanut. An ant has six legs and two feelers on their head. The feelers smell and touch.
examples: Watch a crow at the window walk, hop and flap. The crow bends their legs at the joints, like you.
A dog smells far more than we do, because so much of a dog's nose is for smelling.
You have a small tailbone at the bottom of your back. Many other animals with a backbone have a tail there.
explanations.context: This card is about body parts in humans and in other animals.
explanations.art: A child with arms out like wings next to a crow with wings open, with the arm bones and the wing bones drawn faintly in matching colours.

explanations.description: Your whole body senses, feels and decides, not only your brain. If your hand touches a hot tawa, the hand jumps back before you even know it is hot. The message goes up your arm to your spine, and straight back to the arm muscles. Your tummy has millions of nerve cells of its own, which feel the food and move it along. Many brain scientists say the brain does the real thinking, and the rest of the body only sends and follows messages.
examples: Your hand jumps back from a hot tawa before you feel the pain.
Your eye blinks by itself when something comes close to it.
Your tummy squeezes food along all day, without you choosing to.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study how the whole body senses and responds
perspectives.explanation: Thinking and deciding happen all through the body. The skin, the spine and the tummy all sense and choose what to do.
The brain does the thinking. The rest of the body has quick, automatic responses, which they call reflexes, not thinking.

explanations.context: This card is about where in your body sensing and deciding happen.
explanations.art: A child's hand jumping back from a hot tawa, with a glowing line running from the hand up the arm to the spine and back.

agreed.text: Each body part helps us do some jobs, and many jobs use several parts together.
agreed.evidence: When one part is stopped, like a thumb taped down or an elbow kept straight, some jobs become slow or impossible.

agreed.text: The body bends at joints, where two bones meet, and muscles pull the bones.
agreed.evidence: Feel your elbow as you bend your arm. The hard bones stay straight and the bending happens at the joint. X-ray pictures show the bones meeting there.

agreed.text: Almost all people have the same kinds of body parts, in many sizes, shapes and colours.
agreed.evidence: Doctors all over the world use the same names for the same parts, because they find them in every body.

challenging.claim: The left hand is the wrong hand. Children should be made to eat and write with the right hand.
challenging.who: A common idea in many families, in India and in other countries
challenging.for: Most people are right-handed, and many customs are made for right-handed people.
challenging.against: About one person in ten is left-handed. Being left-handed is a natural way for a body to be. A left-handed child writes and eats just as well with the left hand.
challenging.context: This card is about left-handed people.

challenging.who: A common idea among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: Our thumbs are very good at pinching small things, and we use them all day.
challenging.against: Monkeys and apes have thumbs too, and chimpanzees use them to pick up and hold things. A giant panda has a wrist bone that works like an extra thumb for holding bamboo.
challenging.context: This card is about thumbs in humans and other animals.

challenging.claim: Grown-ups have more bones than children, because they are bigger.
challenging.for: Grown-ups are much bigger than children, so it seems they need more bones.
challenging.against: A baby has about 300 bones. As the baby grows, many small bones grow together into bigger ones. A grown-up has 206 bones, fewer than a baby.
challenging.context: This card is about how many bones a body has.

big_questions.q: When your thumb was taped, you found new ways to pick things up. Where did the new way come from?
big_questions.hint: Think about how you held the rice with your thumb taped, and who worked out how to do it.

big_questions.q: Which part of your body would you miss most if it stopped working for a day? Why?
big_questions.hint: Think about all the jobs you did this morning, and which parts helped.

big_questions.q: A crow's wing has bones like your arm. Why do you think a crow and a child have such similar bones?
big_questions.hint: Humans and crows are both animals. Think about families, and how cousins can look alike.

big_questions.q: Your body is made of many parts. Is there one part that is really 'you'?
big_questions.hint: If you cut your hair, are you still you? If you lose a tooth, are you still you?

story.title: Paati's Thumb and the Pongal Kolam
story.note: Kavya, her Paati (her grandmother) and her cousin Arjun are made up. The facts are true: a kolam is drawn by pinching rice flour between the thumb and first finger and letting it fall in a thin line, big kolams are drawn at the door for Pongal, ants eat the rice flour, and an ant has six legs and two feelers.
text: It was the morning of Pongal in Madurai. The sky was still grey, and the street was quiet.
Every year, Paati drew the big Pongal kolam outside the front door. Every year, Kavya sat on the step and watched.
But this year Paati had a white cloth tied round her right thumb. She had cut it on a sugarcane knife the day before.
'Paati, who will draw the kolam?' asked Kavya.
'You will,' said Paati. 'You are seven now. I will show you how.'
Kavya's cousin Arjun came out, rubbing his eyes. He was five. 'Can I help?' he asked.
'You can carry the flour,' said Paati. She gave him a small steel bowl of white rice flour.
Paati squatted down by the door. Her knees bent, and her ankles bent, and she sat low and steady on her feet. Kavya squatted beside her.
'Take a little flour in your hand,' said Paati. 'Now hold some of the flour between your thumb and your first finger. Rub them together gently, and let the flour fall.'
Kavya grabbed a big handful of flour in her fist. She opened her hand over the ground. Whoomph! The flour fell in one white heap.
Arjun laughed. Kavya laughed too.
'A fist has no small door,' said Paati. 'Your thumb and your finger make a small door. Only a little flour can get through.'

Kavya tried again. She pinched the flour between her thumb and her first finger. She rubbed them gently and moved her hand along. This time a thin white line came out onto the ground. It wobbled, but it was a line.
'Paati, why don't you do it with your other fingers?' asked Arjun. 'Only your thumb is hurt.'
Paati held up her hand with the tied thumb. She tried to pinch some flour between her first finger and her middle finger. The flour slipped out and fell in lumps.
'My fingers are all well,' she said. 'But without my thumb, they have nothing to press against. A pinch needs a thumb on one side and a finger on the other.'
So Kavya drew, and Paati told her where to go. First Kavya put down rows of dots. Then she drew lines that curled round the dots, round and round, until they made a big flower.
Her neck turned so her eyes could follow the line. Her wrist turned so the line could curve. Her knees ached from squatting.
'Every part of you is helping,' said Paati. 'Your eyes watch. Your wrist turns. Your knees hold you low. And your thumb and finger do the drawing.'
When the kolam was done, Kavya stood up and stretched. Arjun put his hand flat next to Paati's good hand.
'Your hand is big and wrinkly,' he said. 'Mine is small and smooth.'
'Count the fingers,' said Paati.
Arjun counted. 'Four fingers and a thumb. Same as mine!'
'Same parts,' said Paati. 'Different hands. Your hand will grow. Mine has been working for seventy years.'
By the time the sun came up, the neighbours were drawing their kolams too. Up and down the street there were white flowers, stars and lamps on the ground.
Kavya bent down to look at her kolam. A line of tiny black ants was walking along one of her white lines.
'Paati! The ants are eating my kolam!'
'Rice flour is food,' said Paati. 'The ants are our Pongal guests.'

Kavya lay on her tummy and looked closely. Each ant had six legs. Each one had two feelers on their head, which tapped the flour again and again. One ant picked up a tiny bit of flour in her jaws and carried it away.
'She has no thumb,' said Kavya. 'But she can still carry things.'
'Her jaws do the pinching,' said Paati. 'Every animal has their own way.'
Kavya looked at her own thumb and her first finger. She pressed them together, and opened them, and pressed them again.
'My thumb and my finger are a team,' she said. 'Neither one can pinch alone.'
Paati smiled. 'Tomorrow you can draw the kolam again. And the day after, my thumb will be well, and we will draw it together.'
story.epiphany: Kavya sees that a pinch is not done by the thumb alone or by a finger alone, but by the two pressing together. Paati, with all her fingers well but her thumb tied, could not draw the kolam.
ask: Why did the flour fall in a heap when Kavya opened her fist?
Paati's fingers were all well. Why could she not draw the kolam?
Which other parts of Kavya's body helped her draw the kolam?
How were Arjun's hand and Paati's hand alike, and how were they different?
art: A quiet Madurai street at dawn, a grandmother with a white cloth on her thumb squatting at a doorway beside a seven-year-old girl, a small boy holding a steel bowl of rice flour.
A girl's fist opening over the ground and a heap of white flour falling out, with the boy laughing.
Close-up of a girl's thumb and first finger pinching rice flour, a thin white line falling onto the ground.
A small smooth hand laid flat beside a large wrinkled hand on the doorstep, both with four fingers and a thumb.
A finished white flower kolam on the ground with a line of tiny black ants walking along one line, a girl lying on her tummy watching them.

games.title: Which Part Am I? A clue game
games.players: 1 or more players and a reader
games.context: This is a game about what each body part helps you do. The reader reads a clue. The players touch the part on their own body.

items.f: I help you see the world. You have two of me.
I help you hear music and voices.
I help you smell jasmine and dosa. You breathe through me too.
I help you eat, talk and sing.
I am a joint in the middle of your arm. I let your arm bend.
I am a joint in the middle of your leg. I bend when you sit down.
I am short and thick. I press against your fingers to pinch.
I am the joint between your hand and your arm. I let your hand turn.
You stand on me and walk on me. You have two of me.
I am at the back of your foot. I touch the ground first when you walk.
I hold your head up, and I let your head turn to look round.
I cover all of your body. I feel hot, cold and every touch.

rules: Mix the 12 clue cards and put them face down.
The reader reads one clue out loud.
Each player touches the part on their own body, and says its name.
The reader turns the card over and reads the answer. Everyone who was right gets a bean.
When all 12 cards are read, count your beans. With only two of you, the grown-up reads and the child plays, then swap. Playing alone? Try to win all 12 beans.

flow.do: Mix the cards. Give each player a small bowl for beans.
flow.say: I'll read a clue. Touch the part on your body, and say its name.
flow.kid: Listen to the clue. Touch that part.

flow.do: 1. Read each card. 2. Players touch and name the part. 3. Read the answer and give a bean for each right answer.
flow.say: I help you smell jasmine and dosa. You breathe through me too. Which part am I?
flow.kid: Touch the part. Say its name.

good: Elbow, knee and wrist.
The parts that bend.

flow.parent: If your child touches the wrong part, read the clue again slowly and act it out a little.

flow.do: Count the beans, then ask the check question.
flow.say: How many beans? Now one more question.
flow.kid: Count your beans.

check.why: A joint is where two bones meet, and the body bends there. Your knee is a joint in the middle of your leg. Your nose and hair do not bend like that.

setup.art: A pile of clue cards face down on a floor, with small bowls of beans beside two children.
setup.caption: 1. Mix the cards. Give each player a bowl.

setup.art: A grandmother reading a card while two children touch their noses and laugh.
setup.caption: 2. Hear a clue. Touch the part and say its name.

games.title: Move Like Me: animal body cards
games.players: 1 or more players and a reader
games.context: This is a moving game about humans and other animals. Each card asks you to move like an animal. Then you say which of your body parts did the job.

items.f: Flap your arms like a crow's wings.
items.b: Arms. A crow's wing has bones like the bones in your arm.

items.f: Walk on your hands and feet like a cat.
items.b: Hands, feet, elbows and knees. A cat has elbows and knees too.

img.credit: Siya ul haque, CC BY, via iNaturalist

items.f: Swing one arm in front of your face like an elephant's trunk.
items.b: Arm, standing in for a trunk. A trunk is a nose and upper lip joined together.

img.credit: Morten Ross, CC BY, via iNaturalist

items.f: Hop on two feet like a sparrow.
items.b: Legs and feet. Sparrows hop with both feet together.

img.credit: John Brew, CC BY, via iNaturalist

items.f: Wiggle two fingers on your head like an ant's feelers.
items.b: Fingers, standing in for feelers. An ant smells and touches with her feelers.

img.credit: Raja Sekhar Chimirala, CC BY, via iNaturalist

items.f: Stretch your neck up tall like a giraffe.
items.b: Neck. A giraffe's long neck has seven bones, the same number as yours.

img.credit: martin ingemansson, CC BY, via iNaturalist

items.f: Wave your bottom like a dog wagging a tail.
items.b: Hips. You have a small tailbone, but no tail.

img.credit: Ankit Shakya, CC BY, via iNaturalist

items.f: Pick up a sock with your toes, like a monkey.
items.b: Toes. Monkeys can grip with their feet.

items.f: Swim with your arms like a turtle.
items.b: Arms. A sea turtle's flippers have finger bones inside.

img.credit: Tejas M, CC BY, via iNaturalist

items.f: Blink slowly like an owl.

rules: Clear a space on the floor. Mix the 10 cards and put them face down.
The reader reads one card out loud.
Everyone moves like the animal for five seconds.
Then each player says which body part they used.
The reader turns the card over and reads the back. Play until all 10 cards are done.

flow.do: Clear a space. Mix the cards.
flow.say: We're going to move like animals. Then tell me which part of you did the moving.
flow.kid: Move like the animal. Which part did you use?

flow.do: 1. Read each card. 2. Everyone moves for five seconds. 3. Each player names the part they used. 4. Read the back.
flow.say: Flap your arms like a crow's wings! Which part of you is like a crow's wing?
flow.kid: Move like the animal. Name the part you used.

ask.q: Which animal parts are like ours?
good: A crow's wing is like my arm.
A cat has knees and elbows like me.
A giraffe has seven neck bones, like me.

flow.parent: The giraffe card surprises many children: a giraffe's neck is long because each of the seven bones is very long.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: One last question.
flow.kid: Answer the last question.

check.q: A crow's wing has bones like which part of you?
check.why: Inside a crow's wing are bones like the bones in your arm: one long bone near the body, then two thinner ones, then small bones at the tip. The crow flies with them, and you carry and throw with yours.

setup.art: A child flapping both arms like wings beside a picture card of a crow.
setup.caption: 1. Read a card. Move like that animal.

setup.art: A child on hands and knees walking like a cat beside a card of a cat.
setup.caption: 2. Say which of your body parts did the job.

worksheets.title: My Body and What It Does (core)

items.p: Here is a drawing of a child. Say the name of each part, and a grown-up writes it in the box: head, arm, hand, knee, foot.
labels: the round part at the top
the long part from the shoulder to the hand
the part at the end of the arm
the joint in the middle of the leg
the part at the bottom that you stand on
a: the round part at the top: head
the long part from the shoulder to the hand: arm
the part at the end of the arm: hand
the joint in the middle of the leg: knee
the part at the bottom that you stand on: foot
items.why: A strong answer names each part and can touch the same part on their own body.
items.art: A simple drawing of a child standing, with five empty boxes and lines pointing to the head, an arm, a hand, a knee and a foot.

items.p: Draw a line from each part to what it helps you do.
items.why: Each part helps with its own jobs. Feet also help you stand and jump, and your nose also helps you breathe.
items.art: Four parts on the left (eyes, ears, a nose, feet) and four small pictures on the right (a rainbow, a bell, a jasmine flower, a footpath), mixed up.

items.p: Meenakshi, a girl of six, tapes her thumb down. Which job will be the hardest for her?
opts: Picking up a coin from the floor
items.why: To pick up a flat coin, the thumb presses on one side and a finger on the other. Waving and clapping need no pinch, so they stay easy.

items.p: Your elbow is a joint. It lets your arm bend.
items.why: True. The elbow is where the bone of the upper arm meets the bones of the lower arm. Your arm bends there.

items.p: Draw your hand picking up a grain of rice. Colour the thumb red.
items.a: A hand with the thumb and first finger pressing together, a small grain between them, and the thumb coloured red.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the grain held between the thumb and a finger, from two sides.
items.art: An empty box with one grain of rice drawn in the middle.

items.p: Is each part in your head, or in your leg? Sort them.
items.why: Eyes, ears and nose are on your head. Knee, ankle and heel are on your leg. Touch each one on your own body to check.

items.p: Look at the picture: one girl, one crow and one ant. Count all their legs.
items.why: The girl has 2 legs, the crow has 2 legs and the ant has 6 legs. 2 and 2 make 4, and 4 and 6 make 10.
items.art: A girl, a crow and a large ant standing in a row, each with legs clearly drawn.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: in the thumb test, why was doing up a button so hard?
items.a: My thumb could not press on the button. My fingers had nothing to push the button against.
items.why: A strong answer uses what the child felt: the button slipped between the fingers, and there was no thumb on the other side.

items.p: Kavya, aged 7, and her cousin Arjun, aged 5, look at their Paati's hand next to theirs.

views.says: Paati's hand is very different from ours. It is big and wrinkly.
Paati's hand is the same as ours. It has four fingers and a thumb.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other one has right.
items.a: A strong answer sees that both are right. The hands have the same parts, a thumb and four fingers, but they are different sizes and look different.
items.why: Bodies are alike in their parts and different in size, shape and colour. Both children noticed something true.

items.p: Three of these are joints, where your body bends. Which one is not?
items.why: Your knee, elbow and wrist are joints, where two bones meet and the body bends. Your nose does not bend like a joint.

items.p: Rimi, a girl in Class 1 in Guwahati, has a newspaper tube round her elbow. Which can she not do with that hand?
opts: Put a biscuit in her mouth
Pick up a ball from the floor
items.why: With the elbow kept straight, her arm cannot fold, so her hand cannot come back to her mouth. Picking up a ball and waving need no bending at the elbow.

items.p: Put these in order, from the top of your body to the bottom.
items.why: Your head is at the top. Your shoulders are below your neck. Your knees are in the middle of your legs. Your ankles are just above your feet.

items.p: Draw a line from each animal's part to the part of you that is most like it.
items.why: A crow's wing has bones like your arm. A trunk is a nose and upper lip joined together. A paw is a hand or foot. Your small tailbone is where many other animals have a tail.

items.p: A baby has more bones than a grown-up.
items.why: True. A baby has about 300 bones. As the baby grows, many small bones grow together. A grown-up has 206.

items.p: Your thumb is taped down. Draw a tool you could make to pick up a bean.
items.a: Any tool that holds the bean from two sides, like tongs, a clothes peg or two sticks, or one that scoops, like a spoon.
items.why: A strong drawing shows how the tool does the thumb's job: pressing the bean from the other side.
items.art: An empty box with one bean drawn at the bottom.

items.p: Farhan writes with his left hand. His aunt says he should use his right hand. Say what you would tell her, and a grown-up writes it.
items.a: About one person in ten is left-handed. It is a natural way for a body to be, and Farhan writes well with his left hand.
items.why: A strong answer is kind to both Farhan and his aunt, and uses a fact or the bean test: most people are quicker with the hand they use most.

items.p: Here is a drawing of an arm. Say the name of each part, and a grown-up writes it: shoulder, elbow, wrist, thumb.
labels: where the arm joins the body
the joint in the middle of the arm
the joint between the arm and the hand
the short thick finger on the side
a: where the arm joins the body: shoulder
the joint in the middle of the arm: elbow
the joint between the arm and the hand: wrist
the short thick finger on the side: thumb
items.why: A strong answer names each part and bends each joint on their own arm.
items.art: An arm drawn from the shoulder to the fingertips, with four empty boxes pointing to the shoulder, the elbow, the wrist and the thumb.

items.p: Lakshmi touched a hot tawa, and her hand jumped back before she felt the pain.

views.says: My hand decided to jump. My hand and my spine did the deciding.
Only your brain decides. Your hand just followed a message.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other one has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason. The message went from the hand to the spine and straight back, before the brain knew. Many scientists call this a reflex, and some say sensing and deciding happen all through the body.
items.why: Scientists still argue about where deciding happens. Both views use the same fact: the hand moved before Lakshmi knew it was hot.

items.p: What is an elephant's trunk?
opts: A long nose and upper lip joined together
A long tail at the front
items.why: An elephant's trunk is a nose and upper lip joined together. The elephant smells, breathes, drinks and picks things up with the trunk.

items.p: Does each part mostly help you move, or mostly help you sense the world? Sort them.
items.why: Legs, arms and knees move you about. Eyes, ears and nose take in what is around you. Your hands and skin do both.

experiments.title: Thumb Taped: which jobs can your hand still do?
experiments.context: In this experiment you try three everyday jobs with your hand. First you do them with your thumb free. Then a grown-up tapes your thumb down, and you try the same jobs again.
experiments.question: If your thumb is taped down, which everyday jobs can your hand still do, and which become hard?
experiments.predict: Guess first. With your thumb taped, which job will be the hardest: picking up rice, picking up a coin, or doing a button? Which will be the easiest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: You use the same hand, the same three jobs and the same things each time. The only change is the thumb: free the first time, taped the second time.
results_table: Thumb free: easy, slow or could not
Thumb taped: easy, slow or could not

materials.item: paper tape, first-aid tape or cello tape, or a soft strip of cloth
materials.qty: a strip as long as your hand

materials.item: a few grains of raw rice on a steel plate
a shirt or a kurta with buttons

schedule.what: Guess which job will be hardest. Do three jobs with your thumb free. Tape your thumb down and do them again. Put a face for each try. Talk about what you found.

experiments.record: On a sheet, draw the three jobs down the side. For each job, draw a face for thumb free and a face for thumb taped: a smile for easy, a straight mouth for slow, a sad face for could not.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the plate of rice, the bowl, the coin on the floor and the shirt. 2. Show each job once.
flow.say: Here are three jobs. Pick up five rice grains, one by one, into the bowl. Pick up the coin from the floor. Do up one button.
flow.kid: Look at the three jobs. Rice, coin, button.
flow.parent: Put the coin flat on a hard floor, not on a mat. Use the hand your child draws with. Do up the button on a shirt lying flat on the floor, or on a shirt your child is wearing.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess, and to say why. Write the guess down, or let your child draw it.
flow.say: Soon I will tape your thumb down. Which job will be the hardest then? Which will be the easiest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. Which job will be hardest with no thumb? Why?

good: The coin, because it is flat and I can't get under it.
All of them will be easy, because I still have four fingers.

flow.parent: Any guess with a reason is a good guess. Do not say which is right. The test will show.

flow.do: 1. Your child does all three jobs with the thumb free. 2. After each job, your child picks a face: easy, slow or could not. 3. Draw the face on the sheet.
flow.say: First, with your thumb free. Pick up the rice grains. Was that easy, slow, or could you not do it?
flow.kid: Do each job with your thumb free. Was it easy?
flow.parent: With the thumb free, most six-year-olds find all three jobs easy, though the button may be slow. That is fine. It gives us something to compare with.

flow.do: 1. Lay your child's thumb flat against the side of the hand, next to the first finger. 2. Wrap the tape once round the thumb and hand, firm but loose enough to slide a finger under.
flow.say: Now I will tape your thumb down. Tell me if it pinches or hurts, and I will loosen it.
flow.kid: Hold your hand flat. Your grown-up tapes your thumb. Say if it hurts.
flow.parent: The thumb should lie flat along the side of the first finger, so it cannot swing across the hand. Never wrap tape tightly. If the fingertip turns pale or your child says it tingles, take the tape off at once. A cloth strip tied loosely works too.

flow.do: 1. Your child does the same three jobs, in the same order, with the thumb taped. 2. After each job, your child picks a face. 3. Draw the face on the sheet. 4. If a job takes more than a minute, stop and mark it 'could not'.
flow.say: Now the same jobs with your thumb taped. Pick up the rice grains. How did that go?
flow.kid: Do the same jobs again. Your thumb is taped. Was it hard?

good: The coin. I could not get it off the floor.
The button. My fingers could not hold it.

ask.q: Did you find a new way to do any job?
good: I picked up rice between two fingers, like scissors.
I slid the coin to the wall, then lifted it.

flow.parent: Usually the coin and the button become very hard or impossible. The rice gets slow, and children often pinch grains between two fingers like scissors. Every child finds their own ways round, and that is worth talking about too.

flow.do: 1. Take off the tape. 2. Your child pinches one grain of rice with thumb and first finger. 3. Ask what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Your thumb is free again. Pick up one grain now. What did you find out? Why were some jobs so hard?
flow.kid: Pinch one grain with your thumb. What did you find out?

ask.q: Your four fingers were free the whole time. So why was the coin so hard?
good: My fingers had nothing to press against.
To pick it up, the thumb has to push on the other side.

flow.parent: Let your child say it first. Then add: the thumb swings across the hand and presses against a finger. A small thing is held between the two. Without the thumb, the fingers can only press against each other, which works badly.

check.q: With your thumb taped, your four fingers could still move. Why was the coin so hard to pick up?
options: Your fingers had no thumb to press the coin against
The tape made your fingers sleepy
check.why: To pick up a small flat thing, you hold it between your thumb on one side and a finger on the other. The coin did not change. Your fingers were fine. They only had no thumb to press against.

rows: Pick up a coin from the floor

experiments.title: Quick Hands: which hand moves more beans?
experiments.context: In this experiment you move rajma beans from one bowl to another, one at a time, for half a minute. You try with one hand, then with the other hand. Then everyone at home has a turn.
experiments.question: In half a minute, will you move more beans with your writing hand or with your other hand?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which hand will move more beans, or will both move the same? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Each hand gets the same beans, the same bowls, the same half minute, and moves one bean at a time.
results_table: Which hand do they write with?

materials.item: rajma, chana or any big dry beans
a phone timer or a clock with a second hand

schedule.what: Guess. Move beans one at a time with each hand for half a minute. Count. Let everyone at home try.

experiments.record: Draw two bowls for each person, one for each hand. Write the number of beans in each.

flow.do: 1. Put all the beans in one bowl. 2. Put the empty bowl a hand's width away. 3. Ask your child to guess, and why.
flow.say: You will move beans one at a time, for half a minute. Which hand will move more beans? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. Which hand will move more beans? Why?

good: My writing hand, because I use it more.
The same, because both hands have a thumb.

flow.do: 1. Start the timer. 2. Your child moves beans one at a time with the writing hand. 3. Stop at 30 seconds. 4. Count the beans together. 5. Pour them back.
flow.say: Ready? Go! One bean at a time. Stop! Let's count them.
flow.kid: Move beans one at a time. Stop when you hear stop.
flow.parent: Moving one bean at a time keeps the test fair. A child who grabs a handful has to start again.

flow.do: Do the same with the other hand. Count again.
flow.say: Now the other hand. Ready? Go! Stop! How many this time?
flow.kid: Now use your other hand. Go!

flow.do: 1. Everyone at home has a turn with each hand. 2. Write each person's numbers. 3. Ask each person which hand they write with. 4. Talk about what you found.
flow.say: Did everyone move more beans with their writing hand? Was anyone the same with both hands?
flow.kid: Let everyone try. Who moved the most beans?

good: Most people moved more with their writing hand.
Amma was nearly the same with both hands.
Left-handed Chithi moved more with her left hand.

flow.parent: Most people move a few more beans with the hand they write with, because they use that hand more. Some people are nearly the same with both. Results change a little each try, so a difference of one or two beans may be luck.

check.q: Ammu, a girl in Class 1, writes with her left hand. Which hand will most likely move more beans?
check.why: Most people are quicker with the hand they use most. Ammu uses her left hand most, so her left hand will most likely move more beans.

setup.art: Two small steel bowls on a floor, one full of red rajma beans and one empty, with a phone timer beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Put the beans in one bowl and a phone timer nearby.

setup.art: A child's hand moving one rajma bean from the full bowl to the empty bowl.
setup.caption: 2. Move one bean at a time for half a minute. Then use the other hand.

activities.title: Head to Toes: touch it, name it, say its job
activities.context: In this activity you stand in front of a mirror. A grown-up names a body part, and you touch it. Then you say one job that part helps you do.

materials.item: a mirror, if you have one

schedule.what: Touch and name body parts from head to toes. Say a job for each one.

activities.record: Say three body parts and their jobs to someone at home at dinner.

flow.do: 1. Stand with your child in front of a mirror. 2. Name a part slowly, from the head down: head, hair, eyes, ears, nose, mouth, chin, neck, shoulders. 3. Your child touches each one.
flow.say: Touch your head. Now your eyes. Now your chin. Now your shoulders. Good. Let's keep going down.
flow.kid: Listen. Touch each part your grown-up names.

flow.do: Keep going down: arms, elbows, wrists, hands, fingers, thumbs, tummy, back, legs, knees, ankles, feet, heels, toes.
flow.say: Touch your elbow. Now your wrist. Now your knee. Now your ankle. Where is your heel?
flow.kid: Touch your elbow. Touch your knee. Find your heel.
flow.parent: Elbow, wrist, ankle and heel are often new words at six. Say each one twice and let your child point.

flow.do: Point to five parts, one at a time. For each, ask what it helps your child do.
flow.say: What do your eyes help you do? What about your knees? What about your thumb?
flow.kid: What does each part help you do? Say it.

ask.q: What do your knees help you do?
good: Bend my legs.
Sit down, jump and climb stairs.

ask.q: What does your nose help you do?
good: Smell things.
Breathe.

flow.parent: Don't worry if your child says only one job. Ask, 'Anything else?' Most parts help with many jobs.

setup.art: A girl and her mother in front of a mirror, the girl touching her chin while the mother points to her own chin.
setup.caption: 1. Stand at a mirror. Touch each part your grown-up names.

setup.art: The girl bending to touch her ankle, with the word 'ankle' in a small speech bubble from the mother.
setup.caption: 2. Go down to your toes. Then say what each part helps you do.

activities.title: Straight-Arm Snack: what does your elbow do?
activities.context: In this activity a grown-up wraps a newspaper tube round your elbow, so your arm cannot bend. Then you try to eat a snack with that hand.

materials.item: newspaper sheets, or a rolled magazine
a small snack, like a piece of murukku, a biscuit or a slice of banana

schedule.what: Wrap a newspaper tube round one elbow. Try to eat a snack with that hand. Then try with the arm free.

activities.record: Draw your arm with the newspaper tube on it. Draw where the snack got to.

flow.do: 1. Roll three sheets of newspaper (or a magazine) into a thick tube round your child's arm, over the elbow. 2. Tape it loosely, so the arm stays straight.
flow.say: This tube will keep your arm straight. Your elbow cannot bend. Tell me if it is too tight.
flow.kid: Hold your arm out straight. Your grown-up rolls a tube round it.
flow.parent: The tube must cover the elbow, but leave the hand and wrist free. Keep it loose: it should stop bending, not squeeze. If the arm still bends the tube, add a third sheet or a rolled magazine.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess first, and to say why.
flow.say: Your hand is free and your fingers are free. Can you put this snack in your mouth with this hand? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. Can you eat the snack with this hand? Why?

flow.do: 1. Put the snack in the hand with the tube. 2. Your child tries to eat it, using only that hand. 3. Watch together.
flow.say: Try it. Only this hand. What happens?
flow.kid: Try to eat the snack. Use only this hand.

good: My hand could not reach my mouth.
I had to bend down to my hand.
My hand got near my face, but not into my mouth.

flow.parent: With the elbow straight, the hand swings past the face but cannot come close to the mouth. Some children bend over and bring the mouth to the hand. That is a clever new way, and worth praising.

flow.do: Take the tube off. Your child eats the second snack the usual way, and feels the elbow bend.
flow.say: Now the tube is off. Eat the other piece. Put your other hand on your elbow. What does it do?
flow.kid: Eat the snack now. Feel your elbow bend.

check.q: With the tube on, why could your hand not reach your mouth?
check.why: The elbow is a joint, where two arm bones meet. Bones do not bend, so your arm bends at the elbow. With the elbow kept straight, the arm stayed long and the hand could not come back to your mouth.

setup.art: A parent rolling a sheet of newspaper round a child's straight arm, covering the elbow, and taping it.
setup.caption: 1. Roll a newspaper tube round the elbow.

setup.art: A child holding a piece of murukku in the hand of the straight arm, the hand stuck out past her cheek, laughing.
setup.caption: 2. Try to eat the snack with that hand.

activities.title: One, Two or Many? Count your body
activities.context: In this activity you count your body parts and sort them into three groups: parts you have one of, parts you have two of, and parts you have many of.

materials.item: three sheets of paper, marked 1, 2 and MANY
small slips of paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Count body parts. Sort each one onto the 1, 2 or MANY sheet. Count teeth in a mirror.

activities.record: Draw one part on each sheet: one part you have one of, two of, and many of.

flow.do: 1. Put the three sheets on the floor. 2. Name a part. 3. Your child counts it on their own body. 4. A grown-up writes it on a slip, and your child puts the slip on the right sheet.
flow.say: How many noses do you have? One. Put 'nose' on the 1 sheet. How many ears? How many knees?
flow.kid: Count each part on your body. Put it on 1, 2 or MANY.
flow.parent: Good parts to use: nose, mouth, tongue, chin, belly button (one); eyes, ears, arms, elbows, knees, feet (two); fingers, toes, teeth, hairs (many).

flow.do: 1. Your child opens wide at the mirror. 2. Count the teeth together, top row, then bottom row.
flow.say: Let's count your teeth. Top row first. Now the bottom row. How many in all?
flow.kid: Open wide. Count your teeth in the mirror.
flow.parent: Most children of six have about 20 milk teeth, but some are already falling out and new ones are coming. Any number is right for your child.

flow.do: Ask the last question and talk about it.
flow.say: Is there a part that you have none of, but a cat or a crow has?
flow.kid: Which part does a cat have that you don't?

ask.q: Which part does a cat or a crow have that you don't?
good: A tail.
Wings, like a crow.
Whiskers, like a cat.

flow.parent: A nice fact to add: you have a small tailbone at the bottom of your back, where many other animals have a tail.

setup.art: Three sheets of paper on a floor, marked 1, 2 and MANY, with small slips on them reading nose, eyes, ears, fingers.
setup.caption: 1. Count a part. Put it on the 1, 2 or MANY sheet.

setup.art: A child with mouth open wide in front of a mirror, counting teeth with one finger.
setup.caption: 2. Count your teeth in a mirror.

activities.title: Hand Family: draw round every hand at home
activities.context: In this activity you draw round the hand of everyone at home on one big sheet. Then you look for what is the same and what is different.

materials.item: a big sheet of paper, or a few sheets of newspaper taped together

schedule.what: Draw round everyone's hand on one sheet. Count the fingers. Find the biggest and the smallest hand.

activities.record: Keep the hand sheet. Write each person's name inside their hand.

flow.do: 1. Each person lays one hand flat on the paper, fingers spread. 2. Your child draws round it with a crayon. 3. Use a different colour for each person.
flow.say: Spread your fingers. Keep still while I draw round your hand. Now you draw round mine.
flow.kid: Draw round each hand. Use a new colour each time.

flow.do: Look at the sheet together. Count the fingers on each hand. Find the biggest and the smallest hand.
flow.say: How many fingers and thumbs does each hand have? Whose hand is the biggest? Whose is the smallest?
flow.kid: Count the fingers on each hand. Which hand is biggest?

ask.q: What is the same about all the hands?
good: They all have four fingers and a thumb.
The thumb is always on the side.
Appa's hand is the biggest.
The baby's hand is tiny.
Some fingers are long and thin.

flow.parent: Very rarely a person has a different number of fingers. If someone in your family does, that is a lovely chance to say that bodies differ in many ways.

flow.do: Ask your child to say one thing that is the same and one that is different.
flow.say: Tell me one way our hands are the same, and one way they are different.
flow.kid: Say one same thing and one different thing.

setup.art: A grandmother's wrinkled hand spread flat on a big sheet of paper while a child draws round it with a red crayon.
setup.caption: 1. Draw round each person's hand.

setup.art: A big sheet with five hand outlines in different colours, from a tiny baby hand to a large grown-up hand.
setup.caption: 2. Count the fingers. Find the biggest and smallest hand.

projects.title: My Body Book: three pages about me
projects.context: In this three-day project you make a small book about your body. Each day you make one page.

materials.item: three sheets of paper, folded in half and stapled or tied with thread

schedule.what: Page 1: draw your whole body. A grown-up helps you write five body parts.
Page 2: 'My hands can…' Draw three jobs your hands did today.
Page 3: 'Same and different'. Draw yourself next to someone at home. Say one way you are the same and one way you are different.

projects.record: The three-page book. Show it to someone and read it to them.

flow.do: 1. Make the book with your child. 2. On page 1, your child draws their whole body. 3. Your child points to five parts, and you help write the names.
flow.say: Draw all of you, from your head to your toes. Which five parts shall we name?
flow.kid: Draw all of you. Name five parts.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child what their hands did today. 2. Your child draws three of those jobs on page 2.
flow.say: What did your hands do today? Did they hold a tumbler, pull a zip, or wave to someone?
flow.kid: What did your hands do today? Draw three things.

ask.q: Which of those jobs needed your thumb?
good: Holding the tumbler.
Pulling the zip.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws themself next to someone at home on page 3. 2. Ask for one way they are the same and one way they are different.
flow.say: Who will you draw next to you? How are you the same? How are you different?
flow.kid: Draw yourself and someone at home. How are you the same?

ask.q: How are you the same, and how are you different?
good: We both have two eyes and ten toes.
Amma is taller, and her hair is longer.

setup.art: Three sheets of paper folded in half and tied with thread into a small book, crayons beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Make a small book.

setup.art: An open page with a child's drawing of herself and labels written by a grown-up: head, arm, hand, knee, foot.
setup.caption: 2. Draw one page each day.

challenges.title: No Thumb? Make a Picker
challenges.context: This is a making challenge. With your thumb taped down, picking up a bean is hard. Can you make a tool that does the thumb's job?
challenges.problem: With your thumb taped, make a tool that picks up five rajma beans, one at a time, and drops them in a bowl.
constraints: Use only things from home: paper, card, ice-cream sticks, clothes pegs, rubber bands, tape, spoons.
Your thumb stays taped the whole time.
Pick up one bean at a time.
materials: rajma beans and two small bowls
a strip of thin card, like a cereal box
general: A spoon that scoops the bean up.
A clothes peg that squeezes the bean, like a thumb and finger.
creative: A strip of card folded in half into tongs, which spring open again.
Two ice-cream sticks with a rubber band round one end and a small folded paper wedge between them.
A loop of tape, sticky side out, round one finger.
challenges.your_turn: Make your own picker. Time how long it takes to move five beans. Then change one thing and try again. Which picker worked best?

flow.do: Read the challenge. Tape your child's thumb loosely, as in the thumb test.
flow.say: Your thumb is taped. Can you make a tool that does the thumb's job, and picks up beans?
flow.kid: Your thumb is taped. Make a tool to pick up beans.
flow.parent: Tape loosely, and take it off at once if the fingertip turns pale or tingles.

flow.do: 1. Your child chooses materials and makes a picker. 2. Help with taping. 3. Try it on five beans.
flow.say: What will you use? How will it squeeze the bean from both sides?
flow.kid: Make your picker. Try it on five beans.

ask.q: How is your picker like a thumb and a finger?
good: It has two sides that press together.
One stick is the thumb and one is the finger.

flow.do: Take off the tape. Your child picks up a bean with thumb and finger and compares.
flow.say: Now pick up a bean with your thumb and finger. Which is faster, your picker or your own hand?
flow.kid: Try your own thumb now. Which is faster?

setup.caption: 1. With your thumb taped, make a picker.

setup.art: A clothes peg, two ice-cream sticks with a rubber band, and a spoon laid next to a bowl of beans.
setup.caption: 2. Try your picker on five beans. Change one thing and try again.

videos.check: No video id was confirmed from here. Choose real footage from Jaipur, short and calm enough for a six-year-old. Check that it credits Ram Chandra Sharma as well as Dr P. K. Sethi.

videos.why: Shows the tip of a trunk gripping something small, the way our thumb and finger pinch.
videos.check: No video id was confirmed from here. Choose real footage of an elephant who is not performing tricks for people.

quiz.p: Which part of your body helps you hear?
quiz.why: Your ears take in sounds, like music and voices.

opts: In the middle of your arm
quiz.why: Your ankle is the joint between your leg and your foot. It lets your foot point up and down.

quiz.p: Which part helps you smell a jasmine flower?
quiz.why: Your nose smells, and you breathe through your nose too.

quiz.p: In the thumb test, why was picking up rice harder with the thumb taped?
opts: The fingers had no thumb to press against
quiz.why: A pinch needs the thumb on one side and a finger on the other. With the thumb taped, the fingers could only press against each other.

quiz.p: Which job needs your thumb the most?
quiz.why: A button has to be pinched from both sides, by the thumb and a finger. Kicking and nodding do not use your thumb.

opts: A place where two bones meet, where you can bend
The hard part of a bone
quiz.why: At a joint, two bones meet. Bones do not bend, so your body bends at its joints.

quiz.p: Which of these is a joint?
quiz.why: Your wrist is where your arm bones meet the bones of your hand. It lets your hand bend and turn.
Muscles get shorter and pull on your bones, and the bones swing at the joints.

quiz.p: All the people at home drew round their hands. What do almost all the hands have?
quiz.why: Almost every hand has a thumb and four fingers. But hands come in many sizes and colours.
An ant has six legs and two feelers. A crow has two legs and a cat has four.

applications: Makers of artificial limbs, like the Jaipur Foot, copy how a real foot bends, so people can walk, squat and climb again.
Doctors called physiotherapists help people move a joint again after an injury, with gentle exercises.
Designers make big buttons, thick pencils and easy-grip handles for people whose thumbs and fingers are stiff, like many older people.
Engineers build robot hands with a thumb that presses against the fingers, so the robot can pick up small things.

open_questions.q: How does a baby's body know where to grow each part?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know many of the signals that tell cells to become a hand or a foot. But how the whole body keeps every part the right size and in the right place is still being worked out.

open_questions.q: Where does deciding happen in a body?
open_questions.why_open: The spine, the tummy and the skin all sense and respond on their own. Scientists still argue about whether to call this thinking, or only the brain's work.

open_questions.q: Why are about one in ten people left-handed?
open_questions.why_open: Left-handedness runs a little in families, but many genes and things before birth play a part. Nobody yet knows the full answer.

ask_kids: Which body parts did you use to eat your breakfast?
Which of your joints bent when you climbed the stairs?
Can you pick up a bit of chapati or dosa without using your thumb?
What does a crow do with their legs and wings?
How are your feet different from a grown-up's feet at home?
Which part of your body do you think works hardest all day?

jokes.j: Why did the skeleton not go to the party?
jokes.a: He had no body to go with!

jokes.j: What has a thumb and four fingers but is not alive?
Why did the elbow go to school?
jokes.a: To learn how to bend the rules!

jokes.j: What do you call a nose with no body?
Why is your nose in the middle of your face?

maths.problem: In a thumb test like yours, Ammu picked up 9 rice grains in one minute with her thumb free. With her thumb taped, she picked up 3. How many fewer grains did she pick up with her thumb taped?
maths.explain: Start at 3 and count on to 9: 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9. That is 6 more. So she picked up 6 fewer grains with her thumb taped, because her fingers had no thumb to press against.
maths.context: This is about the thumb test, where you taped your thumb down and tried jobs like picking up rice. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: Finding the difference shows how much the thumb helped.

maths.problem: Count on your own body: 2 eyes and 2 ears. How many eyes and ears is that in all?
maths.explain: 2 and 2 make 4. You can count them: one eye, two eyes, then one ear, two ears. That is 1, 2, 3, 4.
maths.context: This is about counting body parts and sorting them into one, two and many.
maths.why_maths: Adding parts that come in twos is quicker than counting each one.

maths.problem: Nithya drew round three hands. Her hand was 4 crayons long, Amma's was 6 crayons long, and baby Kuttan's was 2 crayons long. Put the hands in order, from the smallest to the biggest.
maths.explain: 2 is less than 4, and 4 is less than 6. So the order is Kuttan, Nithya, Amma. All three hands have a thumb and four fingers, but they are different sizes.
maths.context: This is about the hand family activity, where you drew round everyone's hand. The lengths are made up.
maths.why_maths: Putting numbers in order shows which hand is the biggest without guessing.

maths.problem: In the bean test, four people said which hand they write with: right, right, left, right. Make a tally. How many write with the right hand, and how many with the left?
maths.explain: Make a tally mark for each answer. Right gets three marks, and left gets one mark. In most families, more people are right-handed, but there is often one left-hander.
maths.context: This is about the bean test, where everyone at home moved beans with each hand. The answers are made up.
maths.why_maths: A tally keeps count of everyone's answer, so you can see which kind is most common.

roots.context: We have named our body parts and found what each one helps us do. Now we ask what the thumb test tells us about where a job really happens.

deep_truth.truth: With your thumb taped down, you could hardly pick up one grain of rice. Your fingers were all still there. A pinch needs a thumb on one side and a finger on the other. So a pinch is done by two parts pressing together.
deep_truth.habit: We give each job to one part: eyes see, legs walk, hands hold. A pinch needs a thumb and a finger together.
deep_truth.evidence: In the thumb test, the fingers were free and could still move, but the coin and the button became very hard or impossible. The rice slipped between the fingers. When the tape came off, the thumb and a finger picked up a grain at once.

three.who_am_i: You are many parts that do things together. Most of what you do happens where your parts meet.
three.what_is_life: A living body is busy all day with parts helping each other: the eyes guide the hands, the knees bend so the feet can climb.
three.what_is_this_world: Humans and other animals have parts like ours, such as a crow's wing bones and a cat's elbows. Each animal uses their parts in their own way.

roots.thread: A pinch needs a thumb and a finger together. A clap needs two hands. A step needs a foot and the ground. Many jobs need two things to meet, and the job fails if one is missing.

teachings.source: Livy, History of Rome 2.32 (the fable of the belly and the limbs)
teachings.teaching: The hands, the mouth and the teeth grew angry with the belly. They said the belly did no work and only ate. So they stopped feeding the belly. Soon the hands, the mouth and the teeth grew weak too. They learned that the belly was doing a job for all of them.
teachings.link: The fable, which Livy says Menenius Agrippa told in Rome, says each part needs the others, which the thumb test shows too. Neither the thumb nor the fingers could pinch alone.

teachings.source: Udana 6.4, a Buddhist text (the blind men and the elephant)
teachings.teaching: Some men who could not see each touched one part of an elephant. The one who touched the trunk said an elephant is like a plough's pole. The one who touched a leg said an elephant is like a pillar. Each was sure he was right, and they began to quarrel.
teachings.link: Each man knew one part, but the elephant was all the parts together. To know a body, we look at the parts and also at how they work together.

science.text: Humans have a long thumb that can press its tip firmly against the tip of each finger. This lets us pinch very small things, like a grain of rice or a thread.
The spine, the gut and the skin sense and respond on their own, without waiting for the brain. Whether to call this thinking is argued about.

other_view.who: The monk Nagasena, in the Buddhist book Milindapanha
other_view.view: Nagasena told King Milinda that a chariot is not the wheels, the axle or the seat, and not something apart from them. 'Chariot' is only the name for the parts put together. He said a person is the same: there is no fixed 'me' to find in any part, or anywhere else.

practice.title: Thumb Hello
practice.say: Sit comfortably and close your eyes. Breathe in slowly, and breathe out slowly. Now touch your thumb to your first finger, gently. Feel where they meet. Now touch your thumb to your middle finger. Now the next finger. Now your little finger. Go back the other way, slowly. Feel each meeting. Breathe in and out once more. Open your eyes.
practice.kid: Close your eyes. Breathe slowly. Touch your thumb to each finger. Go slowly, one finger at a time. Feel each meeting. Open your eyes.

ask: When you clap, which hand makes the sound?
With your thumb taped, you found new ways to pick things up. Who or what found those ways?
Is there any job your body does with just one part, and no help from any other part?

how_we_found_out.context: How do you make an artificial foot that works like a real one? This card tells the true story of the Jaipur Foot.
how_we_found_out.story: In the 1960s, many people in India who lost a leg were given an artificial foot made in the West. It was stiff, and it was made to wear inside a shoe. But many people in India walk barefoot, sit on the floor and squat to cook or work. With a stiff foot, they could not. In 1968, in Jaipur, a craftsman named Ram Chandra Sharma brought an idea to Dr P. K. Sethi, a bone doctor at the city's big hospital. Sharma thought an artificial foot should bend like a real one. A cycle-tyre repairer named Chugga Bhai helped him make the first one from rubber, the way tyres are made. After much testing, they made a rubber foot over a wooden core that bends at the ankle and the toes. People could walk barefoot, squat and even climb trees. This Jaipur Foot is cheap, and is now fitted free for many people. The dancer Sudha Chandran danced Bharatanatyam on stage again with one. Dr Sethi was often named first, and Sharma, the craftsman, is less well known.
how_we_found_out.who: Ram Chandra Sharma, a craftsman, Dr P. K. Sethi, a bone doctor, and Chugga Bhai, a cycle-tyre repairer, in Jaipur
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That an artificial foot only needs to be a stiff support inside a shoe. Ram Chandra Sharma saw that a real foot bends at the ankle and toes, and his rubber foot bent the same way. People could then squat, sit on the floor and walk barefoot.
how_we_found_out.art: A craftsman's workbench in Jaipur with a rubber foot on a wooden core, and beside it a person squatting barefoot on a mud floor wearing the artificial foot.
